contents.text: Nixon ran against two other major candidates in the 1968 election: Vice President Hubert Humphrey and George Wallace, the former governor of Alabama.
Look at the table describing the three major candidates in the 1968 election. Then follow the instructions below.

table.text: Nixon ran on a "law and order" platform to appeal to voters unhappy with social unrest and rising crime. Nixon's voters included business owners, suburban middle-class people, and devoted anticommunists.

Humphrey was Lyndon B. Johnson's vice president, and he campaigned on expanding civil rights and social welfare programs started during the Johnson administration. Humphrey's voters included African American people, members of labor unions, and liberal voters who lived in cities.

George Wallace ran on a platform favoring racial segregation and "states' rights." His votes mostly came from white voters in the South, but he also appealed to some working-class voters in the North.

pieces.text: In October 1969, the largest nationwide protest against the Vietnam War took place. A few weeks later, Nixon responded to the rally and coined one of the most well-known terms associated with his presidency: the
Read the following excerpts from his response. You can use the audio button to hear a recording of Nixon's speech. Then answer the question below.

components.text: In San Francisco a few weeks ago, I saw demonstrators carrying signs reading, "Lose in Vietnam, bring the boys home." Well, one of the strengths of our free society is that any American has a right to reach that conclusion and to advocate that point of view.

But as President of the United States, I would be untrue to my oath of office if I allowed the policy of this nation to be dictated by the minority who hold that point of view and who try to impose it on the nation by mounting demonstrations in the street.

I know it may not be fashionable to speak of patriotism or national destiny these days. But I feel it is appropriate to do so on this occasion.…And so tonight—to you, the great silent majority of my fellow Americans—I ask for your support.
Let us be united for peace. Let us also be united against defeat. Because let us understand: North Vietnam cannot defeat or humiliate the United States. Only Americans can do that.

components.text: In San Francisco a few weeks ago, I saw demonstrators carrying signs reading, "Lose in Vietnam, bring the boys home." Well, one of the strengths of our free society is that any American has a right to reach that conclusion and to advocate that point of view.

But as President of the United States, I would be untrue to my oath of office if I allowed the policy of this nation to be dictated by the minority who hold that point of view and who try to impose it on the nation by mounting demonstrations in the street.

pieces.text: In October 1969, the largest nationwide protest against the Vietnam War took place. A few weeks later, Nixon responded to the rally and coined one of the most well-known terms associated with his presidency: the
Read the following excerpts from his response. You can use the audio button to hear a recording of Nixon's speech. Then answer the question below.

components.text: In San Francisco a few weeks ago, I saw demonstrators carrying signs reading, "Lose in Vietnam, bring the boys home." Well, one of the strengths of our free society is that any American has a right to reach that conclusion and to advocate that point of view.

But as President of the United States, I would be untrue to my oath of office if I allowed the policy of this nation to be dictated by the minority who hold that point of view and who try to impose it on the nation by mounting demonstrations in the street.

I know it may not be fashionable to speak of patriotism or national destiny these days. But I feel it is appropriate to do so on this occasion.…And so tonight—to you, the great silent majority of my fellow Americans—I ask for your support.
Let us be united for peace. Let us also be united against defeat. Because let us understand: North Vietnam cannot defeat or humiliate the United States. Only Americans can do that.

, known as Jimmy Carter, was the 39th president of the United States, serving from 1977 to 1981. Before being elected president in 1976, Carter was a U.S. naval officer, a successful peanut farmer, and a governor of Georgia.

contents.text: Historians often study a person's background to better understand their experiences later in life. Read about Carter's life and career before he became president. Then follow the instructions below.

pieces.text: : Carter is born in Plains, Georgia. His father is a farmer, and his mother is a nurse.
: Carter graduates with distinction from the prestigious U.S. Naval Academy and, one month later, marries Rosalynn Smith.
: Carter addresses difficult challenges while designing one of the U.S. Navy's first nuclear-powered submarines.

: Carter resigns from the navy after his father's death to take over the family farm in Georgia. His first year farming is not profitable, so he adds a peanut-shelling plant and establishes other profitable side businesses.
: Carter is elected to the Georgia State Senate, beginning his political career. He gains attention for attacking wasteful government spending.
: After losing his campaign for governor, Carter takes a break from politics and does Christian missionary work. He begins describing himself as a "born-again" Christian.
: After successfully challenging the sitting governor in the Democratic primary, Carter is elected governor of Georgia and serves until 1975.

: Carter addresses difficult challenges while designing one of the U.S. Navy's first nuclear-powered submarines.

: Carter resigns from the navy after his father's death to take over the family farm in Georgia. His first year farming is not profitable, so he adds a peanut-shelling plant and establishes other profitable side businesses.

contents.text: Amid rising doubts about leadership and a weak economy, the 1976 presidential race offered Americans a clear choice between two very different candidates:

elements.text: As a little-known former governor of Georgia, Jimmy Carter ran as a political outsider and reformer. His pledge to lead with integrity resonated with voters seeking an end to political corruption, while his support for civil rights earned him the backing of many African American voters.

Gerald Ford was the sitting president and former congressman from Michigan. He ran as an experienced leader who understood how to run the federal government. Ford's steady approach to governing appealed to many moderate and independent voters outside the Republican base.

contents.text: Jimmy Carter won the 1976 presidential election, narrowly defeating Gerald Ford. In his 1977 inaugural address, President Carter urged Americans to renew their belief in the nation's core values, which he felt had been damaged by political scandals and a struggling economy.
Read the following excerpts from Carter's inaugural speech. Match each excerpt to the political goal it describes.

draggableItems.text: restore public confidence by requesting teamwork between the leader and the people
encourage people to be realistic about what the government can accomplish
establish the U.S. as a model government by demonstrating a successful democracy
ensure that U.S. policy supports freedom and human rights in other countries

staticItems.text: We have learned that "more" is not necessarily "better," that even our great Nation has its recognized limits, and that we can neither answer all questions nor solve all problems. We cannot afford to do everything.…We must simply do our best.
Let us create together a new national spirit of unity and trust. Your strength can compensate for my weakness, and your wisdom can help to minimize my mistakes.

Because we are free we can never be indifferent to the fate of freedom elsewhere. Our moral sense dictates a clearcut preference for those societies which share with us an abiding respect for individual human rights.

Our Nation can be strong abroad only if it is strong at home. And we know that the best way to enhance freedom in other lands is to demonstrate here that our democratic system is worthy of [imitation].

, known as Jimmy Carter, was the 39th president of the United States, serving from 1977 to 1981. Before being elected president in 1976, Carter was a U.S. naval officer, a successful peanut farmer, and a governor of Georgia.

: Carter graduates with distinction from the prestigious U.S. Naval Academy and, one month later, marries Rosalynn Smith.
: Carter addresses difficult challenges while designing one of the U.S. Navy's first nuclear-powered submarines.

: Carter resigns from the navy after his father's death to take over the family farm in Georgia. His first year farming is not profitable, so he adds a peanut-shelling plant and establishes other profitable side businesses.
: Carter is elected to the Georgia State Senate, beginning his political career. He gains attention for attacking wasteful government spending.
: After losing his campaign for governor, Carter takes a break from politics and does Christian missionary work. He begins describing himself as a "born-again" Christian.
: After successfully challenging the sitting governor in the Democratic primary, Carter is elected governor of Georgia and serves until 1975.

contents.text: Amid rising doubts about leadership and a weak economy, the 1976 presidential race offered Americans a clear choice between two very different candidates:

elements.text: As a little-known former governor of Georgia, Jimmy Carter ran as a political outsider and reformer. His pledge to lead with integrity resonated with voters seeking an end to political corruption, while his support for civil rights earned him the backing of many African American voters.

Gerald Ford was the sitting president and former congressman from Michigan. He ran as an experienced leader who understood how to run the federal government. Ford's steady approach to governing appealed to many moderate and independent voters outside the Republican base.

pieces.text: was the 40th president of the United States, serving from 1981 through the end of his second term in January 1989. He played a major role in reenergizing the conservative movement, focusing on reducing the government's influence on peoples' lives and promoting free market principles.

contents.text: Historians consider an individual's background when studying a public figure. Read the information from Reagan's life and career before he became president. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: Reagan is born in Illinois. His father is a salesman, and his mother is deeply religious.

Reagan enrolls in Eureka College, where he majors in economics while working long hours as a lifeguard to pay for his living expenses. He plays sports, acts in school plays, and is elected student body president.

Reagan works as a radio broadcaster. He sends money home to support his family until his father is hired to oversee a local program created by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Reagan considers himself a Roosevelt Democrat.
Reagan's radio voice impresses Hollywood agents. He begins acting, appearing in more than 50 films between 1937 and 1957.

Reagan is elected president of the Screen Actors Guild labor union, serving until 1954. He cooperates with the FBI to investigate communists in Hollywood and begins to worry about the spread of communism.
As Reagan's acting career starts to decline, he becomes interested in Republican politics. He delivers a speech at the Republican National Convention, launching his political career.

choices.text: His experience with the Screen Actors Guild led him to develop anticommunist views.
His political views developed early and were consistent throughout his life.
He gained strong communication skills as a broadcaster and an actor.
He developed a strong work ethic through working several different jobs.

contents.text: Although Reagan's support for Barry Goldwater in the 1964 presidential election did not lead to a Republican victory, it helped Reagan gain national attention as a rising conservative voice. Just two years later, he was elected governor of California. His leadership helped launch a new era of conservatism. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In the 1970s, a new conservative movement emerged in the United States. It grew in response to the liberal political and social climate of the 1960s, which saw an increase in government social programs, business regulations, and different cultural movements. While many Americans supported these changes, others felt the country had changed too much. Conservatives wanted lower taxes and less government spending and economic intervention. Many conservatives also wanted to preserve their traditional values in the face of social changes, which included issues like affirmative action as well as the hippie and feminist movements of the era. Religious communities were also concerned with the growth of abortion rights and restrictions on school prayer, which they viewed as attacks on their values.

As Reagan's acting career starts to decline, he becomes interested in Republican politics. He delivers a speech at the Republican National Convention, launching his political career.

contents.text: Reagan gave his first major political speech at the 1964 Republican National Convention in support of Barry Goldwater's presidential campaign. His compelling delivery and clear articulation of Republican principles made him an instant favorite within the party, propelling him into the political spotlight.
Read the following excerpt from Reagan's speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: Today, 37 cents out of every dollar earned in this country is the tax collector's share, and yet our government continues to spend 17 million dollars a day more than the government takes in.…We haven't balanced our budget 28 out of the last 34 years.…

Every responsible farmer…has repeatedly asked the government to free the farm economy.…The wheat farmers voted against a wheat program. The government passed it anyway. Now the price of bread goes up; the price of wheat to the farmer goes down.… Outside of its legitimate functions, government does nothing as well or as economically as the private sector of the economy.

contents.text: Although Reagan's support for Barry Goldwater in the 1964 presidential election did not lead to a Republican victory, it helped Reagan gain national attention as a rising conservative voice. Just two years later, he was elected governor of California. His leadership helped launch a new era of conservatism. Read the passage. Then follow the instructions below.

textContent.text: In the 1970s, a new conservative movement emerged in the United States. It grew in response to the liberal political and social climate of the 1960s, which saw an increase in government social programs, business regulations, and different cultural movements. While many Americans supported these changes, others felt the country had changed too much. Conservatives wanted lower taxes and less government spending and economic intervention. Many conservatives also wanted to preserve their traditional values in the face of social changes, which included issues like affirmative action as well as the hippie and feminist movements of the era. Religious communities were also concerned with the growth of abortion rights and restrictions on school prayer, which they viewed as attacks on their values.

contents.text: Although Reagan's support for Barry Goldwater in the 1964 presidential election did not lead to a Republican victory, it helped Reagan gain national attention as a rising conservative voice. Just two years later, he was elected governor of California. His leadership helped launch a new era of conservatism. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In the 1970s, a new conservative movement emerged in the United States. It grew in response to the liberal political and social climate of the 1960s, which saw an increase in government social programs, business regulations, and different cultural movements. While many Americans supported these changes, others felt the country had changed too much. Conservatives wanted lower taxes and less government spending and economic intervention. Many conservatives also wanted to preserve their traditional values in the face of social changes, which included issues like affirmative action as well as the hippie and feminist movements of the era. Religious communities were also concerned with the growth of abortion rights and restrictions on school prayer, which they viewed as attacks on their values.

contents.text: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 presidential election by a wide margin and was inaugurated on January 20, 1981. During his inauguration speech, he outlined goals for his presidency. Read or use the audio button to hear a recording of the excerpt from Reagan's inaugural speech. Then answer the question below.

components.text: These United States are confronted with an economic affliction of great proportions. We suffer from the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history. It distorts our economic decisions, penalizes thrift, and crushes the struggling young and the fixed-income elderly alike. It threatens to shatter the lives of millions of our people.

Idle industries have cast workers into unemployment, human misery, and personal indignity. Those who do work are denied a fair return for their labor by a tax system which penalizes successful achievement and keeps us from maintaining full productivity. But great as our tax burden is, it has not kept pace with public spending. For decades we have piled deficit upon deficit, mortgaging our future and our children's future for the temporary convenience of the present. To continue this long trend is to guarantee tremendous social, cultural, political, and economic upheavals.…
In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.…
To those neighbors and allies who share our freedom, we will strengthen our historic ties and assure them of our support and firm commitment. We will match loyalty with loyalty.…

As for the enemies of freedom, those who are potential adversaries, they will be reminded that peace is the highest aspiration of the American people. We will negotiate for it, sacrifice for it; we will not surrender for it, now or ever.

meaning.text: a financial gap created when a government spends more money than it collects in taxes in a year

contents.text: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 presidential election by a wide margin and was inaugurated on January 20, 1981. During his inauguration speech, he outlined goals for his presidency. Read or use the audio button to hear a recording of the excerpt from Reagan's inaugural speech. Then follow the directions below.

components.text: These United States are confronted with an economic affliction of great proportions. We suffer from the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history. It distorts our economic decisions, penalizes thrift, and crushes the struggling young and the fixed-income elderly alike. It threatens to shatter the lives of millions of our people.

Idle industries have cast workers into unemployment, human misery, and personal indignity. Those who do work are denied a fair return for their labor by a tax system which penalizes successful achievement and keeps us from maintaining full productivity. But great as our tax burden is, it has not kept pace with public spending. For decades we have piled deficit upon deficit, mortgaging our future and our children's future for the temporary convenience of the present. To continue this long trend is to guarantee tremendous social, cultural, political, and economic upheavals.…
In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.…
To those neighbors and allies who share our freedom, we will strengthen our historic ties and assure them of our support and firm commitment. We will match loyalty with loyalty.…

As for the enemies of freedom, those who are potential adversaries, they will be reminded that peace is the highest aspiration of the American people. We will negotiate for it, sacrifice for it; we will not surrender for it, now or ever.

pieces.text: Reagan is born in Illinois. His father is a salesman, and his mother is deeply religious.

Reagan's radio voice impresses Hollywood agents. He begins acting, appearing in more than 50 films between 1937 and 1957.

contents.text: Ronald Reagan won the 1980 presidential election by a wide margin and was inaugurated on January 20, 1981. During his inauguration speech, he outlined goals for his presidency. Read or use the audio button to hear a recording of the excerpt from Reagan's inaugural speech. Then answer the question below.

components.text: These United States are confronted with an economic affliction of great proportions. We suffer from the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history. It distorts our economic decisions, penalizes thrift, and crushes the struggling young and the fixed-income elderly alike. It threatens to shatter the lives of millions of our people.

Idle industries have cast workers into unemployment, human misery, and personal indignity. Those who do work are denied a fair return for their labor by a tax system which penalizes successful achievement and keeps us from maintaining full productivity. But great as our tax burden is, it has not kept pace with public spending. For decades we have piled deficit upon deficit, mortgaging our future and our children's future for the temporary convenience of the present. To continue this long trend is to guarantee tremendous social, cultural, political, and economic upheavals.…
In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem; government is the problem.…
To those neighbors and allies who share our freedom, we will strengthen our historic ties and assure them of our support and firm commitment. We will match loyalty with loyalty.…

As for the enemies of freedom, those who are potential adversaries, they will be reminded that peace is the highest aspiration of the American people. We will negotiate for it, sacrifice for it; we will not surrender for it, now or ever.

meaning.text: a financial gap created when a government spends more money than it collects in taxes in a year

pieces.text: Reagan is born in Illinois. His father is a salesman, and his mother is deeply religious.

Reagan enrolls in Eureka College, where he majors in economics while working long hours as a lifeguard to pay for his living expenses. He plays sports, acts in school plays, and is elected student body president.

Reagan works as a radio broadcaster. He sends money home to support his family until his father is hired to oversee a local program created by President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Reagan considers himself a Roosevelt Democrat.
Reagan's radio voice impresses Hollywood agents. He begins acting, appearing in more than 50 films between 1937 and 1957.

Reagan is elected president of the Screen Actors Guild labor union, serving until 1954. He cooperates with the FBI to investigate communists in Hollywood and begins to worry about the spread of communism.
As Reagan's acting career starts to decline, he becomes interested in Republican politics. He delivers a speech at the Republican National Convention, launching his political career.

contents.text: Since the late 1940s, American foreign policy had been defined by the Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union. But the Soviet Union's power had declined through the 1980s and by 1990, the U.S. was the world's sole superpower. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was the first major test the U.S. faced in the post-Cold War era.

On September 11, 1990, President George H.W. Bush gave a televised address to a joint session of Congress. He outlined the situation in Kuwait and his vision for the U.S. in what he called a "new world order." The video shows portions of President Bush's speech to Congress. Use the video or the transcript to answer the question below.

textContent.text: We stand today at a unique and extraordinary moment. The crisis in the Persian Gulf, as grave as it is, also offers a rare opportunity to move toward an historic period of cooperation. Out of these troubled times…a new world order can emerge: a new era—freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace. An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony.…A world in which nations recognize the shared responsibility for freedom and justice. A world where the strong respect the rights of the weak.…

The test we face is great, and so are the stakes. This is the first assault on the new world that we seek, the first test of our mettle. Had we not responded to this first provocation with clarity of purpose, if we do not continue to demonstrate our determination, it would be a signal to actual and potential despots around the world.…America and the world must stand up to aggression—and we will. And one thing more: In the pursuit of these goals, America will not be intimidated.…

Recent events have surely proven that there is no substitute for American leadership. In the face of tyranny, let no one doubt American credibility and reliability. Let no one doubt our staying power. We will stand by our friends.

A broad international alliance led by the U.S. works together to restore peace and ensure that Iraq withdraws from Kuwait.
Bush encourages Kuwait's neighbors to solve the crisis among themselves so the U.S. can focus on its domestic issues.

contents.text: Since the late 1940s, American foreign policy had been defined by the Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union. But the Soviet Union's power had declined through the 1980s and by 1990, the U.S. was the world's sole superpower. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was the first major test the U.S. faced in the post-Cold War era.

On September 11, 1990, President George H.W. Bush gave a televised address to a joint session of Congress. He outlined the situation in Kuwait and his vision for the U.S. in what he called a "new world order." The video shows portions of President Bush's speech to Congress. Use the video or the transcript to answer the question below.

textContent.text: We stand today at a unique and extraordinary moment. The crisis in the Persian Gulf, as grave as it is, also offers a rare opportunity to move toward an historic period of cooperation. Out of these troubled times…a new world order can emerge: a new era—freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace. An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony.…A world in which nations recognize the shared responsibility for freedom and justice. A world where the strong respect the rights of the weak.…

The test we face is great, and so are the stakes. This is the first assault on the new world that we seek, the first test of our mettle. Had we not responded to this first provocation with clarity of purpose, if we do not continue to demonstrate our determination, it would be a signal to actual and potential despots around the world.…America and the world must stand up to aggression—and we will. And one thing more: In the pursuit of these goals, America will not be intimidated.…

Recent events have surely proven that there is no substitute for American leadership. In the face of tyranny, let no one doubt American credibility and reliability. Let no one doubt our staying power. We will stand by our friends.

contents.text: Since the late 1940s, American foreign policy had been defined by the Cold War rivalry with the Soviet Union. But the Soviet Union's power had declined through the 1980s and by 1990, the U.S. was the world's sole superpower. Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was the first major test the U.S. faced in the post-Cold War era.

On September 11, 1990, President George H.W. Bush gave a televised address to a joint session of Congress. He outlined the situation in Kuwait and his vision for the U.S. in what he called a "new world order." The video shows portions of President Bush's speech to Congress. Use the video or the transcript to answer the question below.

textContent.text: We stand today at a unique and extraordinary moment. The crisis in the Persian Gulf, as grave as it is, also offers a rare opportunity to move toward an historic period of cooperation. Out of these troubled times…a new world order can emerge: a new era—freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace. An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony.…A world in which nations recognize the shared responsibility for freedom and justice. A world where the strong respect the rights of the weak.…

The test we face is great, and so are the stakes. This is the first assault on the new world that we seek, the first test of our mettle. Had we not responded to this first provocation with clarity of purpose, if we do not continue to demonstrate our determination, it would be a signal to actual and potential despots around the world.…America and the world must stand up to aggression—and we will. And one thing more: In the pursuit of these goals, America will not be intimidated.…

Recent events have surely proven that there is no substitute for American leadership. In the face of tyranny, let no one doubt American credibility and reliability. Let no one doubt our staying power. We will stand by our friends.

Iraq's invasion of Kuwait was the first major test the U.S. faced in the post-Cold War era.

On September 11, 1990, President George H.W. Bush gave a televised address to a joint session of Congress. He outlined the situation in Kuwait and his vision for the U.S. in what he called a "new world order." The video shows portions of President Bush's speech to Congress. Use the video or the transcript to answer the question below.

textContent.text: We stand today at a unique and extraordinary moment. The crisis in the Persian Gulf, as grave as it is, also offers a rare opportunity to move toward an historic period of cooperation. Out of these troubled times…a new world order can emerge: a new era—freer from the threat of terror, stronger in the pursuit of justice, and more secure in the quest for peace. An era in which the nations of the world, East and West, North and South, can prosper and live in harmony.…A world in which nations recognize the shared responsibility for freedom and justice. A world where the strong respect the rights of the weak.…

The test we face is great, and so are the stakes. This is the first assault on the new world that we seek, the first test of our mettle. Had we not responded to this first provocation with clarity of purpose, if we do not continue to demonstrate our determination, it would be a signal to actual and potential despots around the world.…America and the world must stand up to aggression—and we will. And one thing more: In the pursuit of these goals, America will not be intimidated.…

Recent events have surely proven that there is no substitute for American leadership. In the face of tyranny, let no one doubt American credibility and reliability. Let no one doubt our staying power. We will stand by our friends.

The U.S. should avoid foreign military commitments in order to focus on domestic issues.
The U.S. should act alone without the approval or assistance of any other countries.
The U.S. should lead a broad international alliance to ensure global peace and cooperation.

content.text: This map shows the countries that sent troops to join the Gulf War coalition led by the United States and indicates how many troops they contributed to the coalition. Several other countries supported the coalition without sending troops: Germany and Japan contributed funds, and Turkey allowed coalition forces to use its airbases to stage attacks.

alternativeText.text: A map of the countries of the world. Countries that contributed troops to the international coalition are shaded according to how many troops they sent. It shows that the United States sent more than 200,000 troops. The United Kingdom and Saudi Arabia sent between 20,000 and 199,999 troops. Canada and France sent between 2000 and 19,999 troops. Afghanistan, Argentina, Australia, Niger, and the Philippines all set less than 2000 troops.

content.text: The Arab League was founded in 1945 to support cooperation between Arabic-speaking countries in the Middle East and North Africa, including Iraq and Kuwait. On August 4, 1990, the Arab League voted on a resolution to condemn Iraq's invasion of Kuwait. This map shows how countries voted on the resolution and whether they contributed troops to the coalition forces.

alternativeText.text: A map of the countries of the Arab League. It shows that Bahrain, Egypt, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Syria, the United Arab Emirates, and Kuwait all voted for the resolution condemning Iraq's invasion of Kuwait and joined the international coalition.   Algeria, Djibouti, Lebanon, Somalia, and Tunisia voted for the resolution.   Jordan, Mauritania, Sudan, Yemen, and Iraq voted against the resolution.   Libya did not vote.

(1990–1991) was a conflict in the Persian Gulf region between Iraq and a coalition of nations led by the United States. When historians study a war, they take into account the historical
, or circumstances, leading up to the event. Read about the context that led to the Gulf War. Then answer the question below.

became the leader of Iraq in 1979. Seeking to expand Iraq's power in the Middle East, Hussein ordered the invasion of Iran in 1980. The U.S. considered Iran to be a hostile nation, so it supported Iraq's invasion by providing military aid and intelligence despite concerns about Hussein's history of human rights abuses. The Iran–Iraq war ended with no clear winner in 1988.

textContent.text: The war left Iraq deeply in debt, particularly to wealthy Arab nations like Kuwait. Hussein pressured Kuwait to forgive these debts, arguing that Iraq had protected the entire region from Iranian expansion. He also accused Kuwait of hindering Iraq's postwar economic recovery by stealing Iraqi oil.

Despite diplomatic attempts to resolve the growing tension, Hussein ordered the invasion of Kuwait on August 2, 1990. Within two days, Kuwait was taken over completely. After this rapid conquest, U.S. leaders worried that Saudi Arabia, an important American ally, would be Iraq's next target.
